From drivers to state-of-the-art algorithms, and with powerful developer tools, ROS has what you need for your next robotics project.

A former robotics hiring manager says many companies don't use ROS, but it is so entrenched in the industry that most solutions look similar enough for skills to transfer. They recommend having ROS experience and demos ready if you want to get into robotics.

ROS has some fundamental design flaws, but it integrates most development software from various research areas. Many sub-projects were abandoned decades ago, and only ROS developers keep these components operational.

After 10 years in robotics: companies refuse to work with anything touching ROS. Most successful production systems that use ROS have a large non-ROS core with a thin ROS layer on top for compatibility. Companies using ROS needed several times the resources of those that don't to achieve the same thing.

There's no reason to skip ROS as a student, since every replacement is ROS-like and ROS terminology is the lingua franca. But the antibodies triggered by even mentioning ROS show how much it is not a fun thing to learn or work with.

Hobbyists, academics and garage startups should use ROS; it will take you from nothing to something faster than anything. But once you ship your first product, plan to migrate off ROS to a custom framework. The commenter has spent years building a custom ROS replacement at a large company, with good results.

Workaround: start with ROS but strictly separate it from your business logic, and avoid depending on the launcher, so you can switch away later. ROS is great for prototyping but not for production. Too many formats to master (XML, launch, msg files, YAML, CMake) when one format would do.
Would love to drop ROS2 to escape the dependency hell and convoluted build system. But there are so many existing ROS nodes and drivers that alternatives face a chicken-and-egg adoption problem.

ROS is dying on the industry front: dependency hell, resource-heavy on embedded systems, too slow for real-time high-speed control loops, and the nav stack is hobbyist-maintained and behind the state of the art. It also shuttles data across processes when AI workloads need to stay in GPU memory, and decentralized messaging was the wrong call.
Nav2 is fine for typical wheeled robots like those listed in its docs, but not useful for more dynamic robots (legged, agile platforms).

With the ROS UR controller running at around 200Hz, blocking the control loop (even down to 100Hz) caused errors. UR3e arms occasionally had massive acceleration spikes and physically crashed into surroundings before e-stopping.
As a ROS2 user: it is terrible. If it's easier to write your own stack, do it, because it will be easier to maintain long term. The conceptual design (nodes) is great; the execution is awful.

Average code quality in ROS is rock-bottom. It contains everything you'd want from a robotics framework, but you pay dearly for it. Running control loops through distributed nodes is a recipe for disaster, and ROS heavily encourages this.

A ROS 1/2 user since 2010 says ROS gives you important things for free if you follow its conventions: data bagging, visualization, teleop and sim. However, the Open Robotics-supplied debs aren't suitable for most product deployments.
ROS setup, build and package boilerplate feels like overkill for new minimal projects. Yet they often end up wanting bags, viewers and CLI tools. LLMs are pretty good at handling the ROS boilerplate.

ROS's async pub/sub isolates components but moves the complexity to system integration. Deploying a ROS-based system is about as hard as rewriting it as a monolith, and it is non-deterministic and hard to debug. Adopting DDS to 'industrialize' ROS missed that the protocol wasn't why industry uptake was low.

Before ROS, each robotics team had to dedicate a sub-team to building and maintaining middleware, which was a waste. ROS might not be perfect, but it's so much better than anything else that exists, and it's open source.

ROS's modularity and serialisable, recordable messages deliver a lot of value in large, multi-machine systems. But pub/sub is too general a concurrency model and a poor fit for real-time and safety-critical systems, which makes productionising harder.

Struggling to learn ROS systematically: tutorials are all over the place and unorganized. Replicating them locally produces all kinds of weird errors, and the naming (tf2, MoveIt!, overloaded 'controller' terms) is confusing.

ROS is popular because packages share common message definitions (e.g. vision_msgs). Object recognition and planning libraries can then interoperate without constantly writing glue code for complex robotics datatypes.
Robotics is already hard, and adding ROS, which almost everyone uses, leaves you disappointed and unenthusiastic. ROS does not make robotics a single bit more enjoyable or easy; quite the opposite.

Services implement a request/response pattern. A client sends a request, and a server replies with a response.
